meta.title: Portfolio — codeberg
meta.description: Two projects where software ends in a physical object: FORM, a pipeline from a drawn cup profile to a printable mother mould, and the parametric structures my workshops built at full scale.

title:
work that
stands up
intro: The projects I am proudest of all ended with something coming off a machine. FORM is the one I am building now: you draw a cup profile and it carries that shape through to tooling a printer can make. The parametric structures came first — workshops where the model had to survive being cut, numbered and assembled by hand.

heroImage.alt: FORM's studio: the unwrapped wall of a tumbler beside a 3D preview of the cup with its relief, and a casting assistant reporting how the mould splits

paragraphs.label: The problem
paragraphs.text: A cup with a relief on it is easy to draw and hard to make. The plaster mould has to come off the model, so every piece of ornament has to clear its own draft angle before anything is printed. In a normal workflow you find that out at the mould, once the modelling is already done.

paragraphs.label: What I built
paragraphs.text: One chain from a drawn section to printable tooling, with the manufacturing check sitting inside each step rather than at the end. You draw a profile and it revolves a watertight solid; wall, capacity and foot resolve live. Ornament is generated on device from a prompt, and a depth model I post-trained turns that picture into a 16-bit height map you judge flat and in the round before accepting it. A draft check then reports how much of the wall is still locked once the mould is split, and at what angle, and a casting assistant eases the relief back until the pieces will release.

aside.label: Where it landed
aside.text: In development. A mug currently comes out as six body pieces plus a base, arranged to fit the print bed.

aside.label: Stack
aside.text: TypeScript, React, Next.js, Three.js, Python, FastAPI, diffusion + depth models, STL

paragraphs.text: Before the code I taught parametric design for three years — architects and students with no programming background, learning to build their own tools in Rhino and Grasshopper. Three of those workshops ended with something standing at full scale: two summers at the Gdynia Summer School and one in Piła.

My part was the workflow and everything between the model and the finished structure. I taught it, co-authored the Grasshopper and Python definitions, and prepared the cut files: nesting, sheet thickness, cutter kerf, joint tolerance, and the numbered assembly order. Then we put the structures up together. They were designed and built with my students.

The rib shell holds by friction alone — every slot sized to real sheet thickness plus kerf, so each numbered rib has to be tapped home and stays there. The panel system is less forgiving: the error at each bolted edge joint accumulates, and the last panel only fits if the tolerances were right. The Piła canopy came out of a simulation that let gravity pull a surface spanned between the trees, then penalised it until every piece could be cut flat.
